newsitem.title: USA: New Year's resolution No. 1 -- save money.
newsitem.headline: New Year's resolution No. 1 -- save money.

text.p: After weeks of spending, wouldn't it be a welcome change to get something for free?
No way, you say. There's no such thing as a free lunch. Everything comes with strings attached.

This is true in many cases. But if you read the fine print, pay attention to details, are flexible with your time and willing to compromise, you may indeed find not only a free lunch, but a free vacation during which to eat it.
"American corporations are literally willing to give things away to get you interested," including computers, pet foods and fashions, said Eric Gershman, a financial communications expert.
Gershman and the staff of Financial Answers Network Inc., his company, have compiled the book, "400 Steals Beyond Belief," or the essential almanac to a freer world.
"Under normal circumstances, companies will give services away to promote their businesses -- this is totally legitimate," Gershman said from his office in Boston.
Such freebies might include pantyhose, candy, canned beverages or toiletries sent to consumers who write to complain or praise the product.

Some companies will offer freebies to entice consumers to spend more. Such sales incentives are designed to build customer loyalty. Like free samples in the supermarket, a little taste is often enough to get customers to buy more in the future.

One of Gershman's favourite freebies is at Crested Butte, Colo., where the ski area has been offering free skiing between Thanksgiving and Christmas since 1990. The area also offers free "never ski" ski lessons during this time.
For children's clothes or accessories, try calling the 800 number on the hang tag of clothes and toys, he says.
"Companies are looking for loyalty" and if they see you are a good customer, they will buy it with free goodies or coupons -- what Gershman calls "cash."

For cheap, or free, vacations, he suggests contacting cruise lines and offering to teach an on-board seminar on your subject of expertise. The pay is often a free cruise. Once you get to a vacation destination, there could be a plethora of freebies just by contacting the local Visitor and Convention Bureau.

You could eat free in a restaurant by working as a restaurant critic, get free shoes by being a shoe tester, get free land from the U.S. government or get free software from computer companies. It just takes a phone call or letter to the proper sources, he said.

Other freebies -- concerts or shows. Gershman says that if you volunteer to be an usher at your local theatre or repertory company, you can see the performance for free, saving the ticket price of $50 or more.
"Free" doesn't always mean "free." Sometimes it means "a lot less expensive." One tip Gerstman offers regards credit cards.

Consumers can get lower rates on their credit cards or lower banking fees by simply requesting it. It is a good idea to mention that the customer could move her account to the competition if the rate is not made more competitive.
"Customer service reps have all sorts of new power to retain us as a customer," he said, advising that if you feel your rates are too high, call and ask to have them lowered.
There are pitfalls to playing the freebie game. Legitimate consumer companies will give services away under certain circumstances to promote their business. But beware of the unscrupulous ones.

Beware of unsolicited freebies, which might come in the form of time shares or credit cards sent, unsolicited, through the mail. Gershman said that in the two years it took to research the book, he didn't come across many scams.
However, should you feel you have been scammed, there's free expert advice from the National Fraud Information centre (1-800-876-7060).
Gershman said he and his researchers did not accept any money from any company when researching the book.
"It's really legit," he said. "We had no agenda other than to make some money on the book."
Of course, some items go out of date, and Gershman said the book will be updated in late 1997.
"400 Steals Beyond Belief" can be ordered by calling 1-800-411-6789, or by writing Financial Answers Network Inc., 129 South Street, Boston, MA 02111. The book sells for $12.
